name: Capital Markets Products
title: Markets Specialist
blurb: Murex and Calypso consulting means configuring how banks price, book, settle and collateralise these products, so knowing each product and its trade lifecycle is the core of the role.

chapters.title: Money markets and day counts
chapters.read: An introductory financial markets textbook's chapter on money-market instruments (deposits, T-bills, CP, call money), simple interest and day-count conventions (ACT/360, ACT/365, 30/360).
chapters.produce: Write a small Excel or Python calculator that returns interest for any amount, rate, dates and day-count convention, and test it on 10 cases in USD, GBP and JPY.

quiz.q: You place ¥100,000,000 on deposit at 0.5% for 91 days, ACT/365. How much interest do you earn? (nearest yen)
A USD 10,000,000 deposit pays 4.0% for 90 days on an ACT/360 basis. How much interest does it pay in USD?
A rate of 5.00% quoted ACT/360 is converted to an equivalent ACT/365 rate. What is that rate in %? (2 decimals)
quiz.ex: Same interest for the same days: 5.00 × 365/360 = 5.069%, about 5.07%.

quiz.q: Under ACT/360, the year fraction for an interest period is:
opts: 30 days per month divided by 360
Actual days divided by the actual days in that year
Actual days in the period divided by 360
Number of months divided by 12
quiz.ex: ACT/360 counts actual calendar days and divides by a fixed 360.

quiz.q: Which day-count convention is standard for GBP money-market deposits?
opts: ACT/365
ACT/360
Number of months / 12
quiz.ex: GBP (like JPY) money markets use ACT/365 Fixed, while USD and EUR use ACT/360.

quiz.q: Which of these is a money-market instrument?
opts: A 10-year government bond
Ordinary shares
A 30-year mortgage
A 3-month treasury bill
quiz.ex: Money markets cover short-term borrowing and lending, typically one year or less.

chapters.title: FX spot and forwards
chapters.read: A financial markets or FX textbook's chapter on quotation conventions (base/quote currency, pips), spot value dates, cross rates and forward pricing by covered interest parity.
chapters.produce: Build a forward calculator that takes spot, two interest rates with their day counts and a tenor, and outputs the outright forward and the forward points; reproduce 5 USD/JPY and EUR/USD examples.

quiz.q: USD/JPY spot is 150.00. JPY interest is 0.40% (ACT/365) and USD interest is 4.40% (ACT/360). What is the 92-day outright forward? (2 decimals)
USD/JPY spot is 150.00, the 1-year JPY rate is 0.5% and the 1-year USD rate is 4.5% (both simple annual, 1 full year). What is the 1-year forward? (2 decimals)
EUR/USD is 1.1000 and USD/JPY is 150.00. What is the EUR/JPY cross rate?
quiz.ex: EUR/JPY = EUR/USD × USD/JPY = 1.10 × 150 = 165.00.

quiz.q: A quote of USD/JPY 150.00 means:
opts: 1 JPY costs 150 USD
1 USD costs 150 JPY
100 JPY cost 150 USD
The forward is 150 points above spot
quiz.ex: The first currency (USD) is the base currency, and the price is in the second (JPY).

quiz.q: Under covered interest parity, the currency with the higher interest rate trades, against the lower-rate currency, at:
opts: A forward premium
A forward discount
Exactly the spot rate
A rate set only by expected future spot
quiz.ex: The higher-rate currency is worth less in the forward market, which offsets its interest advantage. Otherwise there would be riskless arbitrage.

quiz.q: What is the standard spot settlement date for most currency pairs?
opts: The same day for all pairs
One month after the trade date
T+2 (two business days after the trade date)
quiz.ex: Most pairs settle T+2. USD/CAD is a well-known T+1 exception.

chapters.title: FX swaps and FX options
chapters.read: An FX or derivatives textbook's chapters on FX swaps (near and far legs, swap points, funding use) and vanilla FX options (calls and puts, strike, premium, payoff at expiry, intrinsic versus time value).
chapters.produce: Draw the payoff diagrams for a bought USD call/JPY put and a bought USD put/JPY call at strike 145, and write out the cash flows of one buy/sell USD/JPY FX swap.

quiz.q: A bank buys USD 10m against JPY spot at 150.00 and sells USD 10m forward at 149.00 (an FX swap). By how many yen does the near-leg JPY amount exceed the far-leg JPY amount?
You buy a USD call/JPY put on USD 1m with a strike of 145, paying a premium of ¥2,000,000. At expiry USD/JPY is 150. What is your profit in yen, net of the premium?
You hold a USD put/JPY call on USD 2m with a strike of 145. At expiry USD/JPY is 140. What is the payoff in yen (before premium)?
An FX swap is:
opts: A near-date exchange of currencies plus a reverse exchange of the same notional on a later date
An exchange of interest payments only, with no principal
The right to exchange currencies at a fixed rate
A single forward contract with no near leg
quiz.ex: An FX swap combines a spot (or near) leg and an opposite forward leg, and is widely used for funding.

quiz.q: What is the maximum loss for the buyer of a vanilla option?
opts: Unlimited
The full notional
The premium paid
Strike × notional
quiz.ex: The buyer can simply not exercise, so the loss is capped at the premium.

quiz.q: A call option is in the money when:
opts: Spot is below the strike
Spot equals the forward rate
Spot is above the strike
Implied volatility is zero
quiz.ex: Exercising a call lets you buy at the strike, which is worth something only if spot is above it.

chapters.title: Bonds: pricing, yield and duration
chapters.read: A fixed-income textbook's chapters on bond cash flows, pricing from yield, yield to maturity, clean versus dirty price and accrued interest, and Macaulay and modified duration.
chapters.produce: Price three JGB-style bonds in a spreadsheet from their yields, compute modified duration, and check the duration estimate against a full reprice for a 10bp move.

quiz.q: A 3-year bond has a face value of 100, pays a 2% annual coupon and yields 3% (annual compounding). What is its price? (2 decimals)
A 5-year zero-coupon bond with a face value of 100 yields 1% (annual compounding). What is its price? (2 decimals)
A bond has a modified duration of 7. Its yield rises by 0.10%. What is the approximate % change in its price?
A 2-year bond pays a 5% annual coupon and yields 5% (so its price is 100). What is its Macaulay duration in years? (2 decimals)
When market yields rise, the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond:
opts: Falls
Rises
Stays the same, because the coupon is fixed
Rises only for zero-coupon bonds
quiz.ex: The fixed cash flows are discounted at a higher rate, so the price falls.

quiz.q: A bond trades above par (price above 100). This means:
opts: Its coupon rate is lower than its yield to maturity
It must be a zero-coupon bond
It has defaulted
Its coupon rate is higher than its yield to maturity
quiz.ex: Investors pay a premium for coupons that are above the market yield.

chapters.title: Repos
chapters.read: A money-markets or fixed-income textbook's chapter on repurchase agreements: legs, repo rate, haircuts, general versus special collateral, and how JGB repo is used for funding.
chapters.produce: Write out both legs of a 7-day JGB repo (cash amounts, dates, collateral) as you would see them in a trade ticket, including the haircut and repurchase price.

quiz.q: A bank borrows ¥1,000,000,000 in a 7-day repo at 0.20% (ACT/365). How much repo interest does it pay? (nearest yen)
A USD repo of $50,000,000 runs 30 days at 5.0% (ACT/360). How much is the repo interest in USD? (nearest dollar)
Bonds with a market value of $10,200,000 are repoed with a 2% haircut, where cash = market value × (1 − haircut). How much cash is lent?
In a repo, the party that sells the securities now and agrees to buy them back later is:
opts: Lending cash
Borrowing cash
Selling credit protection
Acting only as the clearing house
quiz.ex: A repo is economically a secured loan. The seller of the securities receives cash and posts the securities as collateral.

quiz.q: From the other side, a reverse repo means:
opts: Borrowing cash against securities collateral
Lending cash against securities collateral
Selling securities outright with no buy-back
Swapping fixed for floating interest
quiz.ex: The reverse repo party buys the securities and agrees to resell them, so it is lending cash.

quiz.q: Why is a haircut applied in a repo?
opts: To pay the broker's commission
To compensate the borrower for lost coupons
Because the law requires repo cash to equal exactly the bond's face value
To protect the cash lender if the collateral falls in value or the borrower defaults
quiz.ex: The haircut is a buffer of collateral value over the cash lent.

chapters.title: Interest rate swaps, caps, floors and swaptions
chapters.read: A derivatives textbook's chapters on plain-vanilla interest rate swaps (fixed and floating legs, netting, pricing from discount factors, par swap rate) and on caps, floors and swaptions as options on rates.
chapters.produce: Price a 3-year annual fixed-for-floating swap from given discount factors in a spreadsheet, and write one paragraph explaining when a client would buy a cap versus enter a payer swap.

quiz.q: A JPY swap has a notional of ¥10,000,000,000, a fixed rate of 0.80% and a floating fixing of 0.50% for a 182-day period, ACT/365, with payments netted. How much does the fixed payer pay net? (nearest yen)
Discount factors are DF1 = 0.99, DF2 = 0.97 and DF3 = 0.95. What is the 3-year par swap rate with annual fixed payments, in %? (2 decimals)
A cap has a strike of 1.0% on a ¥100,000,000 notional. The reference rate fixes at 1.5%, and the period's year fraction is 0.25. What does the cap pay for that period, in yen?
A 'payer' interest rate swap means you:
opts: Pay fixed and receive floating
Receive fixed and pay floating
Pay floating in two currencies
Pay an upfront premium for an option
quiz.ex: The swap is named after the fixed leg. A payer pays fixed.

quiz.q: A payer swaption gives its holder:
opts: The obligation to enter a receiver swap
The right to receive fixed at the strike
The right, but not the obligation, to enter a swap paying fixed at the strike rate
A guaranteed floating rate below the strike
quiz.ex: A payer swaption is an option on a payer swap, and it is valuable if rates rise above the strike.

quiz.q: An interest rate floor mainly protects:
opts: A floating-rate borrower against rates rising
A fixed-rate borrower against rates falling
A floating-rate lender or investor against rates falling
An equity investor against share price falls
quiz.ex: A floor pays when the reference rate goes below the strike. A cap protects borrowers against rising rates.

chapters.title: TONA and the LIBOR transition
chapters.read: Bank of Japan and industry explanatory materials on TONA and risk-free reference rates, plus overview articles on the LIBOR transition, compounding in arrears and the ISDA fallbacks.
chapters.produce: Compute compounded-in-arrears TONA interest for one month of daily fixings in a spreadsheet (with weekend weighting), and write a short comparison of TONA, SOFR, SONIA and €STR.

quiz.q: Interest on ¥10,000,000,000 is compounded in arrears using TONA (ACT/365): 0.10% for 1 day, then 0.20% for 3 days (over a weekend), then 0.10% for 1 day. What is the total interest? (nearest yen)
TONA is best described as:
opts: An unsecured overnight call rate published by the Bank of Japan
A secured repo rate published by a clearing house
A 3-month term rate based on panel bank submissions
The Bank of Japan's policy rate as decided at its meetings
quiz.ex: TONA (Tokyo Overnight Average rate) is the average of uncollateralised overnight call rates, and it is the JPY risk-free reference rate.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between overnight RFRs such as TONA and the old LIBOR?
opts: RFRs include bank credit risk, while LIBOR was risk-free
Both were set by the same panel submissions
LIBOR was an overnight rate, while RFRs are 12-month term rates
RFRs are backward-looking overnight rates based on transactions; LIBOR was a forward-looking term rate built from bank submissions and included bank credit risk
quiz.ex: This is why RFR-based products compound overnight rates over the period and why fallbacks add a spread adjustment.

quiz.q: Which currency and risk-free rate pairing is correct?
opts: GBP – TONA
USD – SOFR
EUR – SONIA
JPY – €STR
quiz.ex: The correct pairs are USD–SOFR, GBP–SONIA, EUR–€STR and JPY–TONA.

quiz.q: How does SOFR differ from TONA?
opts: SOFR is unsecured, while TONA is secured
SOFR is secured (based on Treasury repo transactions), while TONA is unsecured
SOFR is a term rate set by panel banks
There is no difference; they are the same rate in different currencies
quiz.ex: SOFR is built from repo transactions collateralised by US Treasuries. TONA is the uncollateralised call rate.

quiz.q: Under the ISDA fallbacks for LIBOR derivatives, the fallback rate is:
opts: The last LIBOR fixing, held constant forever
The central bank policy rate with no adjustment
Zero
The compounded-in-arrears RFR plus a fixed spread adjustment
quiz.ex: The fallback is the relevant RFR compounded in arrears plus a spread adjustment based on the historical LIBOR–RFR difference.

chapters.title: Credit, equity and commodity derivatives
chapters.read: A derivatives textbook's chapters on credit default swaps (premium leg, protection leg, recovery), equity forwards and options, and commodity futures (contango, backwardation, storage costs).
chapters.produce: Make a one-page product sheet for each of CDS, equity option and commodity future, with the cash flows, who uses it and why, and one worked numeric example each.

quiz.q: You buy CDS protection on USD 10,000,000 at a spread of 120bp per year, paid quarterly, ACT/360. What is the premium for a 91-day quarter in USD? (nearest dollar)
The reference entity defaults, and the recovery rate is 40%. On a USD 10,000,000 CDS, how much does the protection seller pay (cash settlement)?
A share trades at ¥2,000. The 1-year simple interest rate is 1%, and a ¥30 dividend will be paid at the 1-year maturity date. What is the fair 1-year forward price?
quiz.ex: F = 2,000 × 1.01 − 30 = 2,020 − 30 = ¥1,990 (the forward holder does not receive the dividend).

quiz.q: The buyer of CDS protection:
opts: Pays a regular premium and is compensated if the reference entity has a credit event
Receives a regular premium and pays out on default
Owns the reference entity's shares
Pays only if the reference entity's rating improves
quiz.ex: A CDS works like insurance against default, with the buyer paying the premium leg.

quiz.q: A bought put option on a stock gains value when:
opts: The share price rises
The dividend is cancelled
The share price falls
Implied volatility falls, holding everything else equal
quiz.ex: A put is the right to sell at the strike, so it is worth more the lower the share price. (Cancelling the dividend raises the forward and lowers the put's value.)

quiz.q: A commodity futures curve is in contango when:
opts: Futures prices are below spot
The spot price is zero
Futures prices are above the spot price, often reflecting storage and financing costs
Futures cannot be physically delivered
quiz.ex: Contango means an upward-sloping curve. Backwardation is the opposite.

chapters.title: Trade lifecycle and operations
chapters.read: An introduction to bank operations: the roles of front, middle and back office, and the post-trade lifecycle (trade capture, confirmation and matching, settlement and SSIs, nostro reconciliation), alongside vendor overview material on how Murex or Calypso maps these steps.
chapters.produce: Draw a swimlane diagram of an FX forward's life from execution to reconciliation, showing which office and which system does each step and which control catches which error.

quiz.q: A bank's USD nostro opened at $5,000,000. It expected an incoming $2,000,000 and an outgoing $1,500,000 that day. The correspondent's statement shows a closing balance of $5,300,000. How large is the reconciliation break in USD?
quiz.ex: Expected close = 5,000,000 + 2,000,000 − 1,500,000 = 5,500,000. Statement = 5,300,000, so the break is $200,000 (for example, part of the incoming payment has not arrived).

quiz.q: Which function typically owns independent P&L verification and monitors market-risk limits?
opts: Middle office (risk management and product control)
Front office (the traders)
Back office settlements
Human resources
quiz.ex: Middle office provides an independent check on the front office's positions, P&L and risk.

quiz.q: In a trading system such as Murex or Calypso, 'trade capture' means:
opts: Sending the cash payment on the value date
Agreeing the month-end general ledger balance
Archiving the trade after maturity
Booking the trade's economic details into the system when the trade is executed
quiz.ex: Capture is the first step: getting the deal into the system so that risk, P&L and downstream processing can start.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of trade confirmation?
opts: To calculate the trader's bonus
Both counterparties agree the trade's economic terms, which catches booking errors before settlement
To decide the market price of the trade
To move the trade to the accounting ledger at year-end
quiz.ex: Confirmation and matching check that both sides booked the same deal.

quiz.q: A nostro account is:
opts: An account another bank holds with us ('your account with us')
An account our bank holds with another bank, usually in a foreign currency ('our account with you')
A trader's personal account
An account used only for equity trades
quiz.ex: Nostro means 'ours'. The account a correspondent holds with us is a vostro.

quiz.q: Which order of post-trade steps is correct?
opts: Settlement → trade capture → reconciliation → confirmation
Confirmation → settlement → trade capture → reconciliation
Reconciliation → confirmation → trade capture → settlement
Trade capture → confirmation → settlement → reconciliation
quiz.ex: You book the trade, agree it with the counterparty, settle it, and then reconcile what actually moved.

chapters.title: Collateral, margin and hedge accounting
chapters.read: Overview material on the ISDA Master Agreement and the Credit Support Annex (thresholds, minimum transfer amount, eligible collateral, haircuts, variation versus initial margin), plus an IFRS 9 hedge accounting summary from an accounting firm's guide.
chapters.produce: Write a step-by-step margin-call worked example under a CSA, and a one-page summary comparing fair value hedges and cash flow hedges with one journal entry each.

quiz.q: Under a CSA, your exposure to the counterparty is ¥120m. You already hold ¥80m of collateral, the counterparty's threshold is ¥20m and the minimum transfer amount is ¥10m. How much collateral do you call, in yen?
quiz.ex: Required = 120 − 20 = 100m; already held 80m; call = 20m, which is above the 10m MTA, so call ¥20,000,000.

quiz.q: You must cover ¥50,000,000 of exposure with JGBs that receive a 2% haircut. What market value of JGBs must be delivered? (nearest yen)
What is the CSA (Credit Support Annex)?
opts: An annex to the ISDA Master Agreement that sets collateral terms such as eligible collateral, thresholds and minimum transfer amounts
A separate trade confirmation for each swap
A central bank regulation on capital ratios
An accounting standard for derivatives
quiz.ex: The ISDA Master Agreement sets the legal framework, and the CSA governs collateral.

quiz.q: How does variation margin differ from initial margin?
opts: Variation margin covers potential future exposure, while initial margin covers current mark-to-market
They are the same thing
Variation margin covers current mark-to-market exposure, while initial margin covers potential future exposure if the counterparty defaults
Initial margin is paid only at maturity
quiz.ex: VM moves with daily MTM. IM is a buffer for the close-out period after a default.

quiz.q: A bank swaps its fixed-rate bond issue to floating to hedge changes in the bond's fair value caused by interest rates. Under IFRS 9 this is a:
opts: Cash flow hedge
Net investment hedge
Fair value hedge
Relationship that can never qualify for hedge accounting
quiz.ex: Hedging the exposure to changes in the fair value of a recognised fixed-rate item is a fair value hedge.

quiz.q: In an IFRS 9 cash flow hedge, the effective portion of the hedging instrument's gain or loss is:
opts: Recognised in OCI (the cash flow hedge reserve) and reclassified to profit or loss when the hedged cash flows affect profit or loss
Recognised immediately in profit or loss
Ignored until the hedge matures
Taken directly to retained earnings, never touching profit or loss
quiz.ex: This matches the timing of the hedging gain or loss with the hedged item. Any ineffectiveness goes to profit or loss.

boss.q: USD/JPY spot is 145.00. The USD rate is 4.0% (ACT/360) and the JPY rate is 0.5% (ACT/365). What is the 181-day outright forward? (2 decimals)
A 2-year bond pays a 3% coupon semi-annually and yields 4% with semi-annual compounding. What is its price per 100 face? (2 decimals)
Bonds with a market value of ¥2,000,000,000 are repoed for 14 days with a 3% haircut (cash = MV × (1 − haircut)) at 0.30% ACT/365. What is the repurchase price in yen? (nearest yen)
The 1-year zero rate is 1.0% and the 2-year zero rate is 1.5% (annual compounding). What is the 1-year rate starting in 1 year (1y1y forward), in %? (2 decimals)
A position of ¥100,000,000 face in a bond priced at 102 has a modified duration of 6. What is its DV01 (value change for a 1bp yield move) in yen?
Using the credit-triangle approximation spread ≈ hazard rate × (1 − recovery), with a hazard rate of 2% per year and a 40% recovery, what is the CDS spread in bp?
A trader books an interest rate swap in the trading system with the pay/receive direction reversed. Which control is most likely to catch this before the first payment?
opts: The annual external audit
The year-end IFRS 9 hedge effectiveness review
Recalculating the trader's bonus
Confirmation matching with the counterparty
boss.ex: Confirmation compares both sides' economic terms soon after the trade, so a reversed direction shows up as a mismatch.

boss.q: A Japanese exporter will receive USD in 6 months and wants to fix the JPY amount now. Which trade fits best?
opts: Buy USD / sell JPY forward for the 6-month date
Sell USD / buy JPY forward for the 6-month date
Enter a JPY payer interest rate swap
Buy CDS protection on its US customer
boss.ex: The exporter is long USD in the future, so it sells USD forward to lock in the yen it will receive. CDS hedges credit risk, not FX risk.

boss.q: Why are collateralised (CSA) and cleared swaps typically discounted on an overnight-rate (OIS/RFR) curve?
opts: Because overnight rates are always higher than term rates
Because the collateral earns an overnight rate, so that rate reflects the funding cost of collateralised cash flows
Because IFRS 9 requires every derivative to use the central bank policy rate
Because collateralised trades have no interest rate risk
boss.ex: With cash collateral that earns the overnight rate, the economically consistent discount curve is the OIS/RFR curve.

boss.q: Interest rates rise sharply across the curve. Which position gains value?
opts: A long fixed-rate bond position
A bought interest rate floor
A bought receiver swaption
A payer swap (pay fixed, receive floating)
boss.ex: A payer swap now receives higher floating payments against a fixed rate locked in when rates were lower. The other positions benefit from falling rates.
